writtenBy: Traditional English song
aboutKids: Someone is waiting and waiting for Johnny to come home from the busy fair, and wonders what is taking him so long.
story: No author is known. A manuscript version dates from the 1770s, and the song was first printed in London in The British Lyre (1792). It was sung at London concerts, appeared in Scottish and Irish collections, and crossed to America within a decade. Its bouncy tune became more famous than its words.
funFact: It reached America so soon after independence that many Americans grew up thinking it was an American song.
catalogNote: Catalog says printed in Edinburgh and London c.1792 via the Scots Musical Museum. Sources confirm a 1792 London printing (The British Lyre); I could not confirm the song itself in the Scots Musical Museum, only Stenhouse's later notes recording Anglo-Scottish circulation. Date and public-domain basis unaffected.

writtenBy: Traditional French-Canadian folk song (author unknown)
origin: Canada (Quebec), possibly with roots in France
aboutKids: Alouette is the French word for a lark, a small brown bird that sings while it flies high up in the sky.
story: Nobody knows who made it up. It was first printed in 1879 in a songbook for students of McGill College in Montreal, and the first known French printing came in 1893. Allied soldiers learned it in France during the First World War and carried it home, and it became a worldwide symbol of French Canada.
funFact: Montreal's professional football team, the Alouettes, is named after this song.
myth: Often said to be a paddling song of the voyageurs, the French-Canadian fur-trade canoeists. That link is a popular theory, not documented; folklorist Marius Barbeau thought the song came from France. The earliest known printing is the 1879 McGill songbook.
catalogNote: Catalog labels it a French-Canadian folk song. Its origin is actually debated: it was first printed in Montreal (1879), but Barbeau believed it originated in France. Public-domain basis unaffected.

writtenBy: Music: Ludwig van Beethoven. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A big, bright, happy tune about joy, that warm feeling when everyone sings together and feels glad inside.
story: This is the main theme from the finale of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824 and printed by Schott in 1826. In the symphony, a choir sings Friedrich Schiller's 1785 poem An die Freude (To Joy). Beethoven was almost completely deaf when he wrote it.
funFact: At the premiere Beethoven could not hear the cheering, so a singer gently turned him around to see the audience clapping.
myth: A popular story says CDs were made 74 minutes long so Beethoven's Ninth would fit. Philips engineer Kees Immink recalled that a long recording of the Ninth was used to justify the length after it had largely been settled, so the symphony was not the real reason.
catalogNote: Catalog public-domain basis says published 1824. 1824 is the premiere; the score was first published in 1826 (B. Schott's Sohne, Mainz). Public-domain status unaffected.

writtenBy: Stephen Foster
aboutKids: A traveller plays his banjo and journeys a long, long way to visit his good friend Susanna.
story: Stephen Foster wrote it in his early twenties; it was first sung in Pittsburgh in 1847 and published in Cincinnati in 1848. Foster was paid just 100 dollars, while dozens of other publishers printed copies of their own. Sheet music sales passed 100,000, a record for an American song at the time.
funFact: Gold seekers heading to California in 1849 sang it so often, with new words about their journey, that it became their unofficial theme song.
catalogNote: Consistent with catalog. Note for content team: the song was written for the minstrel stage and some original verses contain racist language; keep to the first verse and chorus as the catalog specifies.

writtenBy: Traditional French song. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: People hold hands and dance round and round in a circle beside a very old stone bridge in a French town called Avignon.
story: No one knows who wrote it. Some scholars think it goes back to the 15th century, but the evidence is thin. It became famous across France in 1853, when composer Adolphe Adam used it in his comic opera Le Sourd ou l'Auberge pleine. The song is about the Saint-Benezet bridge, finished in 1185.
funFact: The real bridge once had 22 arches across the river Rhone. Floods washed most away, and today only 4 remain, stopping in mid-river.
myth: People are often imagined dancing on the bridge itself, but it was too narrow for that; dances are thought to have taken place on the riverbanks below, which is why some older singers say 'sous' (under) rather than 'sur' (on).
catalogNote: Catalog's '15th-century roots' is a claim repeated by tourism and encyclopedia sources but not firmly documented. One source (Avignon tourism office) even says Adam composed the tune; others say he took up an existing song. Treat the pre-1853 history as uncertain.

writtenBy: Words: Lydia Maria Child. Tune: traditional American, composer unknown
aboutKids: A family rides in a horse-drawn sleigh over the river and through the snowy woods to their grandparents' house for a holiday dinner.
story: Lydia Maria Child, a writer and campaigner, published the poem in 1844 as The New-England Boy's Song about Thanksgiving Day in her book Flowers for Children. It recalls childhood trips to her grandparents' house in Medford, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who set it to music, but it was a classroom favourite by 1900.
funFact: Child's original poem goes to grandfather's house, not grandmother's. The house in Medford, Massachusetts, still stands today.

writtenBy: Words credited to Billy Reeves, music to Frank Campbell (1869 sheet music); also claimed by T. Brigham Bishop
aboutKids: A buzzy little fly keeps zooming around, and we wave our hands and ask it nicely to fly away.
story: The song became a hit on the American stage in 1869. One 1869 sheet music edition credits Billy Reeves for the words and Frank Campbell for the music, arranged by Rollin Howard; T. Brigham Bishop published his own edition the same year and claimed he wrote it. Who really wrote it remains unsettled.
funFact: Its 1869 sheet music described it as a comic song and dance, or walk around.
myth: T. Brigham Bishop said he wrote the song during the Civil War, inspired by a remark from a soldier in his company. This is his own account and has never been independently confirmed.
catalogNote: Catalog credits Bishop with the words and 'Frank Campbell / Billy Reeves' with the music. The 1869 White, Smith & Perry sheet credits Reeves (words), Campbell (music) and Howard (arranger); Bishop's is a separate competing claim. I could not verify that the morning-star last line is the 1869 original (Wikipedia cites it from an 1889 version) or the death dates of Reeves and Campbell. Public domain still holds on the 1869 publication.

writtenBy: Benjamin Hanby (words and music)
aboutKids: Santa's reindeer land softly on the roof, and Santa slides down the chimney with a sack full of toys for the children.
story: Benjamin Hanby wrote it in late 1864 in New Paris, Ohio, for the children in his singing school, because he could not afford printed music. It was published in 1866 by Root and Cady of Chicago in a children's songbook. Hanby died in 1867, aged 33, and was long forgotten as its author.
funFact: It is thought to be the first Christmas song mainly about Santa Claus, and the second-oldest non-religious Christmas song after Jingle Bells.
catalogNote: Catalog public-domain basis says published 1864. Hanby wrote it in 1864; the first publication found is October 1866 (Root and Cady, The Song Birds series). Public-domain status unaffected.

writtenBy: Tune: traditional Welsh. English words: Harold Boulton
aboutKids: A soft, sleepy lullaby that promises a little one they will be cosy, loved and looked after all night long.
story: The Welsh melody Ar Hyd y Nos was first printed in 1784 by Edward Jones, harpist to the Prince of Wales, in his Musical and Poetical Relicks of the Welsh Bards. Sir Harold Boulton wrote the best-known English words in 1884. The Welsh words most sung today are by the poet John Ceiriog Hughes.
funFact: The Welsh title, Ar Hyd y Nos, means exactly the same as the English one: all through the night.

writtenBy: Words: Ernst Anschutz (after August Zarnack). Tune: traditional German. English words: traditional and Little Duet
aboutKids: We sing to a fir tree whose needles stay green and fresh all winter long, even when snow is everywhere.
story: It began as an old German folk song about a fir tree, praised for staying green all year. In 1820 teacher August Zarnack printed a version, and in 1824 Leipzig teacher and organist Ernst Anschutz kept its first verse and added new verses linking the tree to Christmas. It is a Christmas song sung for 200 years.
funFact: Researchers think it may be the very first song to connect the fir tree with Christmas.

writtenBy: Music: Joseph Haydn. English words: Little Duet
origin: London, England (composed by an Austrian composer)
aboutKids: A quiet, tiptoeing tune creeps along softly, and then suddenly goes BOOM with one big loud chord. Are you ready for the surprise?
story: Haydn wrote Symphony No. 94 in London in 1791, during his first visit to England, and led its premiere at the Hanover Square Rooms on 23 March 1792. The gentle slow movement is famous for a sudden loud chord, which gave the whole symphony its nickname, the Surprise.
funFact: Haydn liked this tune so much that he reused it years later in The Seasons, where a farmer whistles it while ploughing.
myth: The loud chord is often said to have been written to wake up sleeping listeners. When his biographer Griesinger asked, Haydn said no: he simply wanted to surprise the public with something new and make a brilliant debut.
catalogNote: Catalog public-domain basis says published 1791. 1791 is the composition year; the premiere was 23 March 1792, and I did not find a 1791 publication. Public-domain status unaffected.

writtenBy: Words: traditional American. Tune: traditional French ('Malbrough s'en va-t-en guerre')
aboutKids: A curious bear climbs all the way over a big mountain to find out what is on the other side. What might he see?
story: The words are traditional and nobody knows who made them up. They are sung to the tune of For He's a Jolly Good Fellow, which comes from the French song Malbrough s'en va-t-en guerre. That tune swept France in the 1780s and later travelled to Britain and America.
funFact: In 1781 a nurse sang this tune while rocking the French royal baby, and Queen Marie Antoinette liked it so much she sang it too.
catalogNote: Catalog dates the words to the 19th century; I found no source dating the bear words, so that remains unconfirmed. The tune facts (French, popular in the 1780s) agree with the catalog.

writtenBy: Words: traditional English. Familiar tune: arranged by Frederic Austin
aboutKids: A friend gives a lovely present for the first day of Christmas: a plump little partridge bird sitting in a pear tree.
story: The words first appeared in Mirth without Mischief, a London children's book from about 1780, as a memory-and-forfeits game: each player repeated the growing list, and a mistake cost a forfeit such as a kiss or a sweet. The tune most people know was arranged by English singer Frederic Austin and published in 1909.
funFact: Children once played it as a memory game. Anyone who forgot a gift had to pay a forfeit, often a kiss or a sweet.
myth: A popular claim says the song was a secret code teaching Catholic beliefs in hiding. Snopes finds no evidence: the claim appears only in the late 20th century, and the supposed meanings were beliefs Catholics and Protestants shared.

writtenBy: Traditional English round, first printed by Thomas Ravenscroft
aboutKids: Three little mice scurry and scamper together, running here and there as fast as their tiny feet can go.
story: It was first printed in 1609 as a round for three voices in Thomas Ravenscroft's songbook Deuteromelia; Ravenscroft may have written it himself. The early words were quite different from today's. The rhyme entered children's books in 1842, and today's familiar words took shape over the following decades.
funFact: Printed in 1609, it is called the earliest printed non-religious song that is still widely known today.
myth: A popular claim says the rhyme secretly describes Queen Mary I and three Protestant bishops. There is no evidence: the bishops were not blinded, the rhyme was first printed decades after her reign, and the earliest words do not match the story.

writtenBy: Traditional American folk song
aboutKids: Someone special is coming to visit, riding all the way around the mountain, and everyone gets ready to cheer and say hello.
story: It grew out of the spiritual When the Chariot Comes, printed in 1899. Poet Carl Sandburg reported that railroad workers in the Midwest sang new words to the melody in the 1890s, and he printed that version in his 1927 collection The American Songbag. Families have kept adding funny verses ever since.
funFact: The first recordings were made in 1924 and 1925 by country singers Henry Whitter and Vernon Dalhart.
catalogNote: Consistent with catalog. The spiritual source and Sandburg's railroad account rest mainly on one source (Wikipedia, citing Sandburg); the 1927 printing is confirmed separately.

writtenBy: Words: John Mason Neale. Tune: 'Tempus adest floridum', traditional
origin: England (tune from the Piae Cantiones collection)
aboutKids: A kind king looks out at the deep snow, sees a poor man gathering sticks, and goes out to bring him food and warmth.
story: John Mason Neale wrote the words in 1853 for Carols for Christmas-tide, edited with Thomas Helmore. They borrowed the tune from a medieval spring song, Tempus adest floridum, printed in the 1582 songbook Piae Cantiones. The carol, sung for over 170 years, is set on St Stephen's Day, 26 December.
funFact: The tune comes from Piae Cantiones, a 1582 songbook compiled by the headmaster of Turku Cathedral School in Finland.
myth: The carol calls him a king, but the real Wenceslas (c. 907-935) was Duke of Bohemia, known for his charity. The royal title was granted after his death by Emperor Otto I.

writtenBy: Attributed to James Yorkston (1884 London edition); otherwise traditional
origin: Ireland (Dublin setting); first printed in the USA and Britain
aboutKids: Molly pushes her wheelbarrow through the streets of Dublin, calling out to everyone that she has fresh cockles and mussels to sell.
story: The song is set in Dublin, but its earliest known printing was in Boston in 1876, in a student songbook. In 1884 a London publisher issued it as a comic song by James Yorkston of Edinburgh, and a variant appeared in Cambridge, Massachusetts the same year. It is now Dublin's unofficial anthem.
funFact: A statue of Molly with her cart stands on Suffolk Street in Dublin, and visitors love to stop for a photo with her.
myth: Molly is often said to be a real 17th-century Dublin fishseller. Historians find no evidence; the 1988 'Molly Malone Day' rested on records of a Mary Malone with no proven link to the song.
catalogNote: Catalog says 'attributed to James Yorkston, published in Cambridge, Massachusetts (1884)'. The Yorkston credit comes from the 1884 London edition (Francis Brothers and Day, arr. Edmund Forman); the 1884 Cambridge, Mass. printing (Students' Songs) is a separate variant, and the earliest known printing is Boston, 1876 (Carmina Collegensia). Public-domain status unaffected.

writtenBy: Words: Robert Burns (from an older song). Tune: traditional Scottish
aboutKids: Old friends hold hands in a big circle and sing together, remembering all the happy times they shared long, long ago.
story: Robert Burns sent the song to the Scots Musical Museum in 1788, calling it an old song, and reworked earlier verses. It was printed in 1796, the year he died, to a slow tune. In 1799 George Thomson matched it with the cheerful melody sung today at New Year around the world.
funFact: In Japan the same tune is played in shops and restaurants to tell customers it is nearly closing time.
myth: It is often treated as wholly Burns's own poem. He reshaped an older song (a 1711 version already had a similar verse and chorus), and his story of taking it down from an old man's singing may have been his own invention.

writtenBy: Harry Dacre (Frank Dean)
aboutKids: Someone sings to their friend Daisy, hoping she will ride with them on a special bicycle with two seats, one behind the other.
story: Harry Dacre, the pen name of Frank Dean from the Isle of Man, took a bicycle to America in 1891 and paid import duty on it. A friend joked that a bicycle built for two would have cost double, and Dacre put the phrase into his song. It became a London music hall hit in 1892.
funFact: In 1961 an IBM computer at Bell Labs sang this song, one of the first songs ever sung by a computer.
myth: It is often said Dacre wrote it about Daisy Greville, Countess of Warwick. This is a popular claim with no firm evidence.

writtenBy: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
aboutKids: A bright, bouncy piece played by violins and other string instruments. Its German name means a little night music.
story: Mozart finished this serenade for strings in Vienna on 10 August 1787, while also working on his opera Don Giovanni. Nobody knows why he wrote it or whether it was played in his lifetime. His widow Constanze sold the manuscript, and it was published around 1827, more than 30 years after his death.
funFact: Mozart's own list says the piece had five movements, but one went missing long ago, so we play only four.
